**Romulus and Remus**
The legendary twin founders of Rome, abandoned as infants and suckled by a she-wolf. In an augury contest Romulus saw twelve vultures to Remus's six and founded the city on the Palatine Hill; he later killed Remus and became Rome's first king.

**Seven Kings of Rome**
Rome was traditionally ruled by seven kings before the Republic: Romulus, Numa Pompilius, Tullus Hostilius, Ancus Marcius, Tarquinius Priscus, Servius Tullius, and Tarquinius Superbus. Numa, the second king, was advised by the nymph Egeria and added January and February to the calendar; Tullus Hostilius destroyed Alba Longa and was said to have been killed by a lightning bolt.

**Tarquin the Proud and Lucretia**
Tarquinius Superbus, the seventh and last king, took power after Servius Tullius was murdered and run over by his own daughter's chariot. He was overthrown in 509 BCE after his son Sextus Tarquinius raped the noblewoman Lucretia, leading to the founding of the Republic. Tarquin is also said to have struck off the heads of the tallest poppies as a silent message to Sextus to kill the leading men of Gabii.

**Sack of Rome by Alaric (410 CE)**
The Visigothic king Alaric sacked Rome in 410 CE, after the execution of the general Stilicho; the Salarian Gate in the Aurelian Walls was opened to let his troops in. The shock of the sack prompted St. Augustine to write The City of God, arguing that Christianity was not to blame.

**Gallic sack and "Vae victis"**
Around 390 BCE, Gauls under Brennus defeated the Romans at the Battle of the Allia and sacked the city. During a dispute over the ransom, Brennus threw his sword on the scales and declared "Woe to the vanquished"; legend says sacred geese warned the defenders of the Capitol, and Marcus Furius Camillus later drove the Gauls off.

**Vandal sack of 455 CE**
The Vandal king Genseric sacked Rome in 455 CE, reportedly invited by Empress Licinia Eudoxia after her husband Valentinian III was assassinated, and angered by the broken engagement of his son Huneric to Valentinian's daughter Eudocia. Later sacks include those by the Ostrogoth Totila in the Gothic War and by Charles V's mutinous troops, including German Landsknechts, in 1527.

**Conflict of the Orders**
The long struggle between Rome's aristocratic patricians and common plebeians in the early Republic. The plebeians staged "secessions," leaving the city en masse; Menenius Agrippa ended one by comparing the social classes to parts of a body, and the conflict formally ended with the Hortensian Law of 287 BCE.

**Twelve Tables**
Rome's first written law code, drawn up around 450 BCE by a ten-man commission (the decemviri) and displayed publicly on bronze tablets. It was a concession to plebeians who wanted the laws written down rather than interpreted solely by patricians.

**Gracchi brothers**
Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, tribunes of the plebs in the late second century BCE who pushed land reform to break up the great estates (latifundia), as in Tiberius's agrarian law. Both were killed by political opponents, marking the start of violence in Roman politics.

**Roman Forum**
The central public plaza of ancient Rome, between the Palatine and Capitoline Hills, home to the rostra speaking platform, the Basilica Aemilia, and the Arch of Septimius Severus. Mark Antony delivered his funeral oration for Julius Caesar there, and the Arch of Titus, depicting the menorah taken from Jerusalem, stands on the nearby Via Sacra.

**Great Fire of Rome**
The fire of 64 CE that began near the Circus Maximus and destroyed much of the city under Nero, who supposedly "fiddled while Rome burned." Nero blamed the Christians, starting the first major persecution, and was rumored to have set the fire to clear space for his palace, the Domus Aurea.

**Edward Gibbon's The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire**
A multi-volume history whose first volume was published in 1776. Gibbon blamed the fall on a loss of civic virtue and the rise of Christianity; the Western Empire ended in 476 CE when Odoacer deposed the last emperor.

**Milvian Bridge and the Tiber**
The Tiber is Rome's river. At the Milvian Bridge over the Tiber, Constantine defeated Maxentius in 312 CE after reportedly seeing a vision of the Christian cross.

**Lateran Treaty and the Vatican**
The 1929 agreement between Mussolini's Italy and the papacy that recognized Vatican City, an enclave within Rome, as an independent state. Rome is the seat of the pope, the Bishop of Rome and head of the Catholic Church.

**March on Rome and the Risorgimento**
Rome became the capital of unified Italy in 1871 following the Risorgimento unification movement. In 1922 Benito Mussolini's Blackshirts staged the March on Rome, which brought him to power as fascist dictator.
